newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis prompts new police shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis prompts new police shake-up.

text.p: Peru's 88-day-old hostage crisis has prompted a new shake-up of senior police chiefs for poor handling of the siege at the Japanese ambassador's home where Marxist rebels are holding 72 men, government sources said on Saturday.

A senior Interior Ministry source told Reuters that the heads of police special operations directorate DINOES and its tactical operations unit (SUAT) were transferred to desk jobs, in part for leaking information to the news media.

"They were transferred due to the closeness they have with reporters in the handling of information," said the source, who spoke on condition of anonymity. "There were no secrets because everything was known."
SUAT chief Col. Juan Carlos Mejia Leon also was ousted for firing tear gas into the diplomatic compound at the start of the crisis on Dec. 17 as well as for speaking to reporters, the source said.

Mejia's boss, DINOES head Col. Julio Santillan Valdivia, was transferred for "a series of errors," including allowing reporters to break through police lines and scurry into the besieged mansion at least twice in the early days of the siege.
Both Santillan and Mejia were transferred to administrative posts in the police Inspector General's Office.
In the early days of the crisis President Alberto Fujimori replaced Peru's two top security chiefs, including the head of the anti-terrorist police DINCOTE, who were among the hostages.
The Peruvian government has several times during the crisis been at odds with the foreign news media.
In the early weeks, a Japanese reporter was expelled from the country after sneaking into the residence with his translator to interview rebel chief Nestor Cerpa.
More recently, a cameraman for a British video news service fled Peru, citing veiled threats by Peru's intelligence service after he spoke by radio with rebels in the compound.

The incident occurred last week after hostage-takers of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) broke off face-to-face talks with the government, charging that security forces were digging a tunnel to storm the mansion and rescue the hostages.
